title: Penhawitz, Sachem of the Canarsie
summary: Penhawitz, also written Penhawis, was a seventeenth-century Indigenous leader associated with the Keshaechquereren and Canarsie world of western Long Island, in what is now Brooklyn.
content:
Penhawitz, also written Penhawis, was a seventeenth-century Indigenous leader associated with the Keshaechquereren and Canarsie world of western Long Island. Dutch colonial records document his role in a 1637 land transaction, but the cited sources do not establish his birth or death dates.

The surviving record is filtered largely through Dutch colonial documents. Penhawitz is remembered through named events and recorded negotiations rather than a complete life story.3

Historical Context

A 1637 sale records that Penhawis and Cakapeteyno had the consent of the Keshaechquereren community to sell Pagganack, now Governors Island, and Brooklyn tracts known in the record as Rinnegaconck.2

Later records connect Penhawitz to broader Canarsie, Flatbush, and New Netherland diplomacy, while debated kinship claims remain outside this biography unless the records support them directly.23

His page is included because western Long Island and Brooklyn are part of the Native Long Island historical landscape, and because his name anchors a specific Indigenous presence in early Dutch land records.1

References

  1. Museum of the City of New York, Penhawitz, mcny.org.
  2. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700, p. 136.
  3. Robert S. Grumet, The Munsee Indians: A History.
why_this_matters: Penhawitz places Canarsie and western Long Island within Indigenous homelands with named leaders, diplomacy, and colonial pressure, not only later Brooklyn neighborhoods.
